Keywords: Phenotype, Overgrowth syndrome, Lui Jee Baron syndrome, SPIN4 gene, Epigenetics

body.p: Large for gestational age (LGA) infants—defined as those with birth weight above the 97th percentile—constitute approximately 3% of all newborns. The genetic underpinnings of LGA are increasingly recognized, with associations reported in rare syndromes such as Pallister-Killian syndrome and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. These disorders typically manifest as generalized or segmental overgrowth during the fetal and/or childhood period, frequently accompanied by tall stature, visceromegaly, and macrocephaly.1

Epigenetic dysregulation has been identified as a key mechanism in the pathogenesis of these overgrowth syndromes, affecting genes that regulate cellular proliferation and chromatin remodeling.1 Spindlin family member 4 (SPIN4), a member of the SPIN/SSTY family, functions as an epigenetic reader and is known to negatively regulate somatic growth in both mice and humans. Loss-of-function mutations in SPIN4 result in enhanced Wnt signaling activity and consequent somatic overgrowth.2

We report a rare case of Binder phenotype in a fetus with a SPIN4 gene mutation, representing the first prenatally diagnosed and only the second case reported in the literature. Ethical approval for this clinical observation was obtained from the Institutional Ethics Committee of VMMC & Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi. Written informed consent was acquired from the patient’s family for the publication of this report and associated clinical images.

A 36-year-old gravida 4, para 1, living 1, abortion 2 (G4P1L1A2) woman of Asian Indian ethnicity, in a non-consanguineous marriage, presented at 22 weeks of gestation with an ultrasound finding of isolated mid-facial hypoplasia in the fetus. First-trimester nuchal translucency and fetal echocardiography were unremarkable; however, biochemical aneuploidy screening was not performed. The couple exhibited no clinical signs of mid-facial hypoplasia or relevant medical history. Their first child had normal neurodevelopment.

Based on maternal age, the a priori risk of trisomy 21 was 1 in 205.3 A three-generation pedigree revealed tall stature in both the maternal uncle and sibling (Supplementary Fig. S1, http://links.lww.com/MFM/A92). Following pre-test genetic counseling, the couple consented to amniotic fluid karyotyping, chromosomal microarray analysis, and whole exome sequencing (WES).

Karyotyping and chromosomal microarray analysis were normal, with no pathogenic copy number variants. WES revealed a likely pathogenic X-linked hemizygous frameshift variant, c.648_649delTG, in exon 1 of the SPIN4 gene (Tudor domain), resulting in the amino acid substitution p.Gly217fs*16 (Supplementary Table 1, http://links.lww.com/MFM/A92).

Sequencing was performed using next-generation sequencing platforms covering approximately 30 Mb of the human exome, targeting ~99% of consensus coding sequence and RefSeq regions, with a mean depth of 80–100X and > 90% of bases covered at 20× depth. The variant depth was 23×. GATK best practices were followed, including duplicate read removal, base quality recalibration, and indel-based realignment via the DRAGEN BIO-IT platform (v4.2.4). Variant annotation utilized established databases, including Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man, Genome-wide association studies, The Genome Aggregation Database, and 1000 Genomes.

Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation of the variant: the mother was a heterozygous carrier, and the older sibling was hemizygous and affected (Supplementary Figs. S2 and S3, http://links.lww.com/MFM/A92). At 8 years of age, the sibling had a bone age of 9–11 years (Supplementary Fig. S4, http://links.lww.com/MFM/A92), a height of 147 cm (above the 97th percentile4), normal neurodevelopment, and average academic performance. The mid-parental height was 183 cm.

Serial growth scans every 3–4 weeks showed fetal weight consistently above the 97th percentile (Supplementary Figs. 5A–H, http://links.lww.com/MFM/A92). No evidence of hepatosplenomegaly or chondrodysplasia punctata was noted. The pregnancy was managed by a multidisciplinary team including a maternal-fetal medicine specialist, clinical geneticist, and neonatologist at a tertiary care center with Level III neonatal intensive care unit support (Supplementary Fig. S6, http://links.lww.com/MFM/A92).

At 38+5 weeks, the patient experienced spontaneous labor, delivering a male infant weighing 4.0 kg (97th percentile) with an Apgar score within normal limits. The head circumference was 35 cm (90th–95thpercentile) and length was 52.5 cm (97th percentile).5 The neonate exhibited a flat facial profile, with no other dysmorphic features.

At 6 months of age, the infant is achieving appropriate developmental milestones and is feeding well. His height (73 cm) and weight (10 kg) remain above the 97th percentile according to World Health Organization growth standards.6 Due to geographic limitations, skeletal survey and abdominal ultrasound could not be performed.

Lui-Jee-Baron Syndrome (LJBS) is a rare overgrowth disorder that presents prenatally, characterized by excessive cellular proliferation, tall stature, macrocephaly, and distinctive facial features. In this case, fetal mid-facial hypoplasia—a feature associated with disorders such as autoimmune conditions, vitamin K deficiency, and monogenic syndromes including Keutel syndrome and chondrodysplasia punctata—was the initial clinical indicator.7,8

Unlike previously described overgrowth syndromes caused by mutations in epigenetic writers,9 LJBS is attributed to a mutation in SPIN4, an epigenetic reader. In a seminal study by Lui et al.2, a hemizygous frameshift variant in SPIN4 was identified in a male with tall stature, visceromegaly, and macrocephaly. Functional analysis revealed that wild-type SPIN4 binds modified histone H3, enhances canonical Wnt signaling, and suppresses cell proliferation. In contrast, the mutant SPIN4 protein lacking two of three Tudor-like domains failed to perform these functions, leading to somatic overgrowth. The same variant has also been implicated in colorectal and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, underscoring its potential role in tumorigenesis.9

The large fetal size observed in our case supports the role of SPIN4 in growth regulation. Notably, despite the overgrowth, both our case and the proband described by Lui et al.2 showed normal neurodevelopment, suggesting that intellectual disability may not be a consistent feature of LJBS.

We discussed the reproductive implications of this finding with the family, including a 50% recurrence risk in male offspring. As the natural history becomes clearer, carrier screening and preimplantation genetic testing may be considered in future pregnancies. Consistent with findings from Lui et al.,2 the hemizygous male in our case is expected to have a more pronounced phenotype than the heterozygous mother.

The identification of mid-facial hypoplasia and prenatal overgrowth during anomaly scans, coupled with a likely pathogenic SPIN4 variant, underscores the importance of comprehensive genetic evaluation in similar cases. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first case of Lui-Jee-Baron Syndrome diagnosed prenatally, expanding the phenotypic and diagnostic spectrum of the syndrome.

This case reinforces the value of advanced genomic technologies, multidisciplinary prenatal care, and long-term follow-up in managing rare overgrowth syndromes. Further research is warranted to delineate the full phenotypic spectrum and natural history of SPIN4-associated disorders, which may open avenues for future therapeutic strategies.
